content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a novel procedure to learn an end-to-end SAT solver.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The paper proposes a novel representation of SAT problems for neural-network-based SAT solving. 

2. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve higher accuracy and better generalization compared to NeuroSAT.

Weakness:

1. The experiment still focuses on toy examples and is no way near solving real-world benchmarks.

2. The claim that transformation into AIG reduces diversity in distribution is ill-defined and not well-supported. Why is BR value a good metrics to compare when it comes to diversity?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is overall clearly written. But some claims are not well-justified as discussion above.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while I think the paper presents some interesting ideas. The significance of the work is limited as it still focuses on toy problems and the key claim about the benefit of an AIG representation is not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an end-to-end learning method for SAT problems. A Boolean formula is first transformed into an and inverter graph (AIG) leveraging the knowledge from the electronic design automation field. The observation is that this step reduces the distribution diversity among SAT instances, and facilitates generalization. The distribution of SAT solutions is then seen as a product of conditional Bernoulli distributions. A directed acyclic graph neural network (DAGNN) with two polarity prototypes is trained as a conditional generative model. The DAGNN uses a bidirectional propagation process, that mimics the Boolean constraint propagation essential in SAT solvers. Experimental results show that the new scheme, DeepSAT, performs better on both accuracy and generalization capabilities, compared to existing end-to-end learning-based solutions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
DeepSAT uses the knowledge from Electronic Design Automation to SAT solving, through the use of optimized And Inverter Graphs. This helps with learning and generalization, by reducing the distribution diversity. The use of DAGNN exploits the decomposition of the problem into conditional Bernoulli distributions, and the bidirectional propagation mimics BCP, supporting some interpretability. 

Weaknesses:
The empirical evaluation is only against NeuroSAT, as a representative of end-to-end learning based SAT solvers. The training datasets are still the SR(n) type, introduced by NeuroSAT, which are small, random problems. The tests are performed only on satisfiable problems, because DeepSAT is an incomplete solver. The tests are performed on SR type problems, and on some novel distributions (graph k-coloring, vertex k-cover, k-clique-detection and dominating k-set), with small size, 6-10 nodes. 
Is there any chance that DeepSAT could scale up in the future to problems from SAT competitions, and be compared with traditional solvers?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The main ideas of the paper are clearly presented, and there is some originality in the preprocessing based AIGs, some of the conditional Bernoulli formulation, and the use of DAGNN.
content.summary_of_the_review: DeepSAT is a new end-to-end learning based SAT solver, that leverages EDA knowledge and DAGNN. It performs better on small random problems than NeuroSAT, but it is not apparent if and how these learning based methods could scale.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a machine learning (ML) framework called DeepSAT that targets solving the propositional satisfiability (SAT) problem by means of training and using a graph neural network (GNN). The distinct feature of this work is that the GNN is applied not to the original formulas in conjunctive normal form (CNF) but instead to the and-inverter graphs (AIGs) representing those formulas. For that, the standard conversion of CNF formulas to AIGs is applied followed by a number of circuit processing techniques adapted from the area of electronic design automation (EDA). Experimental results obtained on a range of randomly generated formulas suggest that the proposed ML-based SAT solver outperforms NeuroSAT, which is known to be one of the first attempts to solve SAT by means of the modern ML methodology.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: This paper can be seen as another attempt to develop a purely ML-based solver for an important combinatorial problem. Although the claims made by the authors are quite positive, I am afraid I do not see many pros in this concrete work, so I will discuss some of its weaknesses. The paper has a number of representation, quality and novelty issues detailed below, which in my view clearly prevent it from being accepted.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Let me start by saying that the paper seems to be written in haste and the write-up is sloppy. The authors fail to define a number of important concepts, make mistakes when referring to existing notation and fail to cite seminal works in the area. For instance, SAT is not an "optimization problem" (the authors say that it is). Also, a formula does not "return" anything (the authors say it does). I am not sure what "logic 1/0" is - I guess the authors meant the word "value". The SAT problem consists in determining the existence of an assignment of values to the formula's variables rather than checking if there exists "a combination of inputs".

The concepts mentioned in the text without a proper definition include distribution diversity (how exactly the authors define it and why it is reduced by the AIG representation is left a mystery), relational inductive bias, attention mechanism, and GRU, among a few others. Also, the authors mention and emphasize the word "interpretability" when talking about polarity prototypes - I am not sure what kind of interpretability is meant here and why. Does it have something to do with explainable AI (XAI)?

As for references, BCP had been known long before 2007 and so the authors fail to put a proper reference. When talking about the popularity of CNF formulas, the authors could and perhaps should cite DIMACS, the most popular text format for storing CNFs. AIGs are left without a citation. Finally, when talking about the success story of SAT, the authors fail to cite the most seminal works on clause learning (on the GRASP and Chaff solvers), which are known to be the driving force behind the SAT revolution. I would also recommend the authors check the "Handbook of Satisfiability" and the references therein.

Despite the claims made by the authors, experimental results are relatively weak. First, NeuroSAT has never been a well-performing solver and so considering it as a competitor is somewhat questionable. Granted that ML-based solvers cannot do much nor they realistically compete with the state of the art in SAT solving, I believe the authors could claim some kind of success if their solver was at least on par with ancient solvers like GRASP and Chaff, not to mention something basic but still more-or-less efficient like MiniSat. Second, random CNF formulas are unattractive from a practical point of view. How about solving some of the (simple) industrial instances? They are plenty of them.

I should also say that the EDA techniques mentioned in the title, abstract, introduction, and list of contributions are not detailed anywhere in the text, which makes me wonder why these contributions are claimed. In this regard, I should also say that the performance improvement provided by the AIG format is not explained/discussed in the text. It is given as a fact with no proper analysis. Why does it help? What do you mean by distribution diversity at all, with respect to what is it measured? Does the fact that AIG preprocessing helps mean that CNF formula preprocessing will also help solvers like NeuroSAT? There are plenty of preprocessing techniques readily available for CNF formulas. This should have been discussed in the text.

Finally, the section on "novel distributions" is unclear to me. The authors claim to solve optimization problems by training a GNN to tackle decision (SAT) problems. Do you mean you can somehow find the optimum for the newly created graph optimization problems with a decision oracle (you claim to "solve" them)? If yes, how? If the problems are meant to be decision versions, then this should have been explained. Also, the problem encodings should have been provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: As a result and given the issues I mentioned above, I believe the paper fails to make a sufficiently good contribution that could warrant its acceptance at a flagship AI conference such as ICLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a deep learning framework for SAT.  Their approach uses logic synthesis and masked generative models.  Their experimental results appear competitive with the literature.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The approach appears novel.
2. The experimental results look good when compared to NeuroSAT.

Weaknesses:
1. Major parts of the paper are unclear, including:
   a. Figure 1 is not explained well at all in the caption or in the main text.  There are many things going on, and you seem to expect the reader to automatically know what it all means.
   b. BR is not formally defined, including no definition of "fanin region size", etc.
   c. Figure 2 is not explained well at all either, both in the caption and the main text.
   d. Figure 3 does not describe the algorithm clearly at all.  It's not clear how it works from the figure.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work seems novel and of good quality, but the paper is unclear (see weaknesses above).  


Other comments:
Page 1: The use of "on the one/other hand" is not appropriate here; you are just listing common weaknesses rather than oppositional concepts.

Page 2: "univariate Bernoulli distribution" should be "distributions".

Page 3: At the start of Sec 3.1, you say x_i \in {True, False}, when in fact assignments to x_i come from that set. 

Page 3: "termed as a" -> "termed a" 

Page 3: "following-ups" -> "follow-ups" 

Page 4: Is the exponent in p(x_i ...) correct?  Shouldn't it be (1-\theta_i)^{1-x_i}

Page 5: You say that you filter random assignments that violate conditions, but don't say what happens if every random assignment gets filtered out.

Page 5: How can one expect to generate "all possible satisfying solutions" efficiently? 

Page 5: "an multi-" -> "a multi-"

Page 6: Define "GRU"

Page 6: "we imposes" -> "we impose" 

Page 7: "At t iteration" -> "At iteration t"

Page 7: What does "well-trained DeepSAT" mean? 

Page 8: "k-SAT problem" -> "k-SAT problems"

Page 9: Do solutions to SAT problems derived from other problems (e.g., graph coloring) directly yield solutions to the original problem instances? 

Page 9: Why do raw AIGs include less sturctural information for learning? 

Page 14: "Beside" -> "Besides"

Page 15: Drop parens around "(Li et al.)" and "exampple" -> "example" and "t iteration" -> "iteration t"
content.summary_of_the_review: The results appear good and novel, perhaps sufficiently so for ICLR.  However, many parts of the paper are very unclear, which makes me recommend rejection in its current form.

content.title: DeepSAT: An EDA-Driven Learning Framework for SAT
content.abstract: We present DeepSAT, a novel end-to-end learning framework for the Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problem. Unlike existing solutions trained on random SAT instances with relatively weak supervision, we propose applying the knowledge of the well-developed electronic design automation (EDA) field for SAT solving. Specifically, we first resort to logic synthesis algorithms to pre-process SAT instances into optimized and-inverter graphs (AIGs). By doing so, the distribution diversity among various SAT instances can be dramatically reduced, which facilitates improving the generalization capability of the learned model. Next, we regard the distribution of SAT solutions being a product of conditional Bernoulli distributions. Based on this observation, we approximate the SAT solving procedure with a conditional generative model, leveraging a novel directed acyclic graph neural network (DAGNN) with two polarity prototypes for conditional SAT modeling. To effectively train the generative model,  with the help of logic simulation tools, we obtain the probabilities of nodes in the AIG being logic ‘1’ as rich supervision. We conduct comprehensive experiments on various SAT problems. Our results show that, DeepSAT achieves significant accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art learning-based SAT solutions, especially when generalized to SAT instances that are relatively large or with diverse distributions.
